sentences.text: Bajadasaurus was a large, four-legged herbivore with a long neck, tail, and a relatively tiny head.
This animal possessed extremely elongated, two-pronged neural spines extending from its neck, a feature common in dicraeosaurids where the spine curves forward unlike in Amargasaurus.
As of 2019, the Bajadasaurus skull was the most complete dicraeosaurid skull known to science.
The lower jaw of this dinosaur was approximately 80% the length of its skull.
The most notable anatomical feature of Bajadasaurus is its extremely elongated neural spines on the neck vertebrae that point forward.
A single preserved neck vertebra has an extremely elongated neural spine that is 58 cm long, making the vertebra four times taller than it is long.
The genus name Bajadasaurus derives from the Spanish word bajada referring to the Bajada Colorada site combined with the Greek term saurus meaning lizard.

The only known specimen was excavated in 2010 by paleontologists from the Argentinian National Scientific and Technical Research Council, consisting of an almost complete skull, proatlas, atlas neuroapophyses, axis, and a tentatively identified fifth cervical vertebra.
The specimen was found at the Bajada Colorada locality, 40 km south of Picún Leufú near the Limay River in Patagonia.
Researchers hypothesize that Bajadasaurus could look forward while feeding due to the exposure of its eye openings.
Muscle reconstruction suggests Bajadasaurus was less capable of pulling its head upward compared to Camarasaurus.
The neural spines of Bajadasaurus are highly vascularized and show cyclical growth marks.
Research estimates that Bajadasaurus replaced its teeth on average every 40.7 days.
A 2023 study suggests Bajadasaurus may have had a keratinous beak-like structure supporting its tooth-bearing muzzle, though definitive evidence is missing.
Researchers suggest Bajadasaurus's spines may have supported a neck sail used for display or to deter rivals.
Researchers suggested in 2019 that the elongated spines of Bajadasaurus and Amargasaurus may have served as passive defense against predators.
Bajadasaurus is classified as a genus of dinosaur.
Bajadasaurus belongs to the family Dicraeosauridae, which is one of the three principal families within the sauropod subdivision Diplodocoidea.
Bajadasaurus belongs to the parent group Dicraeosaurinae.
Bajadasaurus lived in northern Patagonia, Argentina, during the Early Cretaceous between 145 and 132.9 million years ago.
Bajadasaurus lived approximately 140 million years ago during the early Cretaceous period, specifically the Berriasian stage.
Bajadasaurus lived from the Berriasian to the Valanginian, approximately 139.1 to 132.6 million years ago.
Bajadasaurus fossils were found in Lower Cretaceous rocks in Patagonia, Argentina.
Bajadasaurus fossils were recovered from the Bajada Colorada Formation.
The sediments of the Bajada Colorada Formation, where Bajadasaurus was found, were mostly deposited by braided rivers.

The Bajada Colorada Formation represents a fluvial and deltaic ecosystem preserving fossils of terrestrial reptiles, including the sauropod Leinkupal laticauda, various theropods including basal tetanurans, and remains possibly belonging to Abelisauroidea and Deinonychosauria.
The locality where Bajadasaurus was found also yielded remains of other sauropods, including Leinkupal laticauda and Ninjatitan zapatai.
Fossils from the Bajadasaurus locality include several species of theropods belonging to basal Tetanurae, and possibly abelisauroids and deinonychosaurians.
While several functions have been proposed for the spines in related Amargasaurus, the 2019 description suggests they served as passive defense in both Bajadasaurus and Amargasaurus.
A 2020 study by Whitlock and Mantilla placed Bajadasaurus as the most basal member of a specific clade within Dicraeosauridae, differing from earlier classifications.
A 2022 study suggests that the spines of Bajadasaurus and other dicraeosaurids likely did not support a keratinous sheath, contradicting earlier beliefs.
